name: Rostrum of the corpus callosum
function: The rostrum is the thin anterior-inferior continuation of the callosal genu toward the lamina terminalis. It contains commissural fibres linking parts of orbital/basal frontal cortex; boundaries of functional callosal territories overlap.

afferent: Commissural axons from basal/orbital frontal cortex of each hemisphere

clinical.findings: May contribute to disconnection in larger anterior callosal/medial frontal lesions; alien-hand behavior is not specific to rostrum.
Partial or complete developmental absence has variable manifestations; associated malformations influence outcome.

name: Genu of the corpus callosum
function: The genu is the anterior bend of the corpus callosum. Fibres sweep forward as forceps minor to frontal cortex, providing interhemispheric frontal communication; exact functional subregions overlap.

afferent: Commissural axons from frontal cortical areas
efferent: Contralateral frontal homotopic and heterotopic targets

clinical.findings: Can contribute to intermanual conflict, apraxia or impaired bimanual coordination, especially with associated medial frontal injury. Not all lesions produce alien hand.
Demyelination, infarction, trauma and developmental abnormalities may involve genu; imaging location alone does not specify the clinical syndrome.

name: Body of the corpus callosum
function: The callosal body is the arch-shaped trunk above the lateral ventricles. It carries interhemispheric fibres, including sensorimotor and parietal connections, with overlapping topography and variable individual organization.

afferent: Commissural axons from bilateral sensorimotor/association cortex
efferent: Contralateral cortical targets; connections include homotopic and heterotopic regions

bloodSupply: Mainly ACA pericallosal branches; posterior callosal territory may overlap PCA supply.

clinical.findings: Lesions can impair bimanual tasks or interhemispheric motor/sensory transfer; signs depend on portion and associated cortical damage.
Surgical interruption can reduce spread of selected seizure types, especially disabling drop attacks; it does not necessarily prevent all bilateral seizures or cause a full split-brain syndrome.

name: Splenium of the corpus callosum
function: The splenium is the thick posterior corpus callosum and carries posterior interhemispheric visual/association connections. Forceps major extends into occipital white matter, while tapetal fibres line parts of the lateral ventricle. The adjacent hippocampal commissure is anatomically distinct.

afferent: Posterior cortical commissural axons from both hemispheres
efferent: Contralateral occipital, parietal and temporal cortical targets

bloodSupply: Mainly PCA splenial/posterior pericallosal branches, with variable ACA overlap.

clinical.findings: A classic pattern follows dominant (usually left) occipital plus splenial injury; visual input from the intact hemisphere is disconnected from reading/language networks.
Infarction, demyelination and cytotoxic splenial lesions can affect transfer or cognition; not every splenial MRI lesion is reversible or an infarct.

name: Internal capsule, anterior limb
synonyms: frontopontine and anterior thalamic radiation segment
function: The anterior limb lies between caudate head medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. It carries anterior thalamic radiation, reciprocal frontal-thalamic fibres and frontopontine projections. It is a projection-fibre corridor, not an independent relay nucleus.

afferent: Anterior/MD thalamocortical projections to frontal/cingulate regions

bloodSupply: ACA/Heubner and MCA lenticulostriate branches with variable overlap.

clinical.findings: May disrupt frontal-thalamic networks and produce executive, motivational or behavioral changes; weakness depends on associated motor-fibre injury.
Capsular/corona-radiata injury can combine contralateral weakness and ataxia on the same affected body side; ataxia is not ipsilateral to the cerebral lesion.

name: Internal capsule, genu
function: The genu is the bend between anterior and posterior limbs, near the caudate-thalamus transition. Corticobulbar projections are conventionally localized to genu/anterior posterior-limb regions, but their precise distribution is not a rigid single compartment.

afferent: Projection fibres from cortical and thalamic motor networks crossing the region
efferent: Corticobulbar/corticoreticular fibres to brainstem motor systems

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA lenticulostriate arteries, with variable ACA/anterior choroidal contributions.

clinical.findings: Can cause contralateral lower facial or tongue weakness and dysarthria; bilateral pathway injury can produce pseudobulbar syndrome.
Can follow pontine or capsular lesions with dysarthria and impaired hand dexterity, sometimes including weakness; not specific to genu alone.

name: Internal capsule, posterior limb
function: The posterior limb lies between thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Motor fibres are conventionally mapped more anteriorly and somatosensory thalamocortical fibres more posteriorly, with overlap and individual variability. Retrolenticular optic and sublenticular auditory radiations are adjacent distinct capsular subdivisions.

afferent: Somatosensory and motor thalamocortical projection fibres
efferent: Corticospinal and associated descending motor projections; corticothalamic return

bloodSupply: MCA lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal branches; superior/inferior and anterior/posterior territories vary.

clinical.findings: Can cause contralateral face-arm-leg weakness, with sensory loss depending on lesion extent. Pure motor hemiparesis is a pattern, not proof of a single location.
Contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss may coexist when the relevant capsule/visual structures are injured; the full triad is not obligatory.
Weakness and disproportionate limb ataxia are on the body side contralateral to a hemispheric lesion; pontine and other sites can cause a similar pattern.

name: Corona radiata
synonyms: corona radiata of the internal capsule
function: The corona radiata is the fan of ascending and descending projection fibres above the internal capsule. The centrum semiovale also contains association and commissural fibres and is not simply synonymous with corona radiata. Fibre overlap complicates inference from a small displayed coordinate.

afferent: Thalamocortical projection fibres to appropriate cortical territories

bloodSupply: Long medullary branches from cerebral cortical arteries and variable deep perforator overlap; some regions are vulnerable to internal border-zone ischemia.

clinical.findings: Can cause contralateral motor/sensory deficits or cognitive changes according to fibres involved.
May produce chains of deep white-matter infarcts with impaired perfusion; lesion pattern and clinical deficits require imaging correlation.
Can involve this region but are not diagnosed from one symptom or atlas location.

name: Arcuate fasciculus
function: The arcuate fasciculus is a dorsal association pathway linking temporal language/auditory regions with frontal and inferior parietal networks. Its relation to subdivisions of the superior longitudinal fasciculus varies by naming convention; it is not identical to the whole SLF. Both sides have related pathways, with variable functional asymmetry.

afferent: Temporal, inferior parietal and frontal association-cortical axons; a bidirectional bundle rather than a relay nucleus
efferent: Reciprocal temporal-frontal/parietal targets in dorsal language and auditory-motor networks

bloodSupply: Subcortical MCA/medullary territories along much of its course, with variable regional and border-zone supply.

clinical.findings: Can impair repetition, phonological processing or speech production; conduction aphasia can reflect cortical or white-matter network injury and is not specific to arcuate interruption.
